National Consumer Disputes Redressal
Ashok Kumar Goel S/O. P.C.Goel vs Yes Securities India Ltd on 22 July, 2026
NATIONAL CONSUMER DISPUTES REDRESSAL COMMISSION
 NEW DELHI
 SECOND APPEAL NO. NC/SA/622/2025
(Against the Order dated 20th August 2025 in Appeal No. SC/7/A/292/2023 of the State Consumer
 Disputes Redressal Commission Delhi)
 WITH
 NC/IA/11624/2025 (EXEMPTION FROM DIM DOCUMENTS)
 NC/IA/11618/2025 (EXEMPTION FROM FILING THE CERTIFIED COPY)
 NC/IA/585/2026 (WAIVER OF COSTS)

ASHOK KUMAR GOEL S/o. P.C.GOEL
PRESENT ADDRESS - 1ST FLOOR ,110-A/4, KRISHNA NAGAR SAFDARJUNG ENCLA ,
SAFDARJUNG ENCLAVE , KRISHNA NAGAR , SOUTH,DELHI.
 .......Petitioner(s)

 Versus

YES SECURITIES INDIA LTD
PRESENT ADDRESS - FIRST FLOOR ,PLOT NO-1/9 , OPPO METRO PILLAR NO-203 , WEST
PATEL NAGAR , NORTH WEST,DELHI.
 .......Respondent(s)

BEFORE:
 HON'BLE DR. INDER JIT SINGH , PRESIDING MEMBER
 HON'BLE MR. SHASHI NANDKEOLYAR , MEMBER

FOR THE PETITIONER:
 MR. ASHOK KUMAR GOEL, IN PERSON (VC)

FOR THE RESPONDENT:
 MS. RADHA SINGH, ADVOCATE (VC)

DATED: 22/07/2026
 ORDER
SHASHI NANDKEOLYAR
1. This Second Appeal, preferred under
Section 51(2)
of the Consumer Protection Act,
2019 ["Act"], assails the Order dated 20.08.2025 passed by the Delhi State Consumer
Disputes Redressal Commission ["Impugned Order"], Delhi in First Appeal No.
A/292/2023, whereby the State Commission, while exercising its appellate jurisdiction,
 upheld the Order dated 31.03.2023 and the Review Order dated 23.05.2023 passed by the
District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission-II, Delhi in Complaint Case No. 10 of
2022, and dismissed the First Appeal preferred by the Appellant. Though the controversy
is modest in its monetary compass, it raises a question of some practical significance to
consumer jurisprudence, namely, whether a service-provider who has collected monies in
advance towards a subscription/brokerage plan, and has admittedly rendered service
commensurate with only a fraction of the said advance, can resist a claim for return of the
unutilized balance on the ground that the consumer has not independently established
"deficiency in service" in the classical, fault-based sense understood in cases involving
disputed allegations of negligent performance.
INTRODUCTION OF THE PARTIES

2.1 Sh. Ashok Kumar Goel ["Appellant"], is stated to be a senior citizen, aged about 75
years, resident of 1st Floor, 110-A/4, Krishna Nagar, Safdarjung Enclave, New Delhi-
110029, who subscribed, for himself and as Karta of "Ashok Kumar Goel, HUF," to an
advance-brokerage plan offered by the Respondent for trading in shares/securities. The
Appellant has appeared in person throughout these proceedings.
2.2 M/s Yes Securities (India) Limited ["Respondent"], having its office at First Floor,
Plot No. 1/9, West Patel Nagar, Opposite Metro Pillar No. 203, New Delhi-110008, is a
stock-broking entity engaged, inter alia, in the business of providing broking, research and
allied advisory services to its subscribers/clients, including the Appellant, for consideration,
and is accordingly a "service provider" within the meaning of
Section 2(42)
read with
Section 2(7)
of the Act, the Appellant being a "consumer" within the meaning of
Section
2(7)
thereof.
BRIEF FACTS OF THE CASE

3.1 On 08.11.2019/11.11.2019, the Appellant subscribed to an advance-brokerage plan
bearing Plan Code "V-13" offered by the Respondent, by paying a sum of Rs. 5,90,000/-
(Rupees Five Lakh Ninety Thousand only), debited from the linked bank account of Ashok
Kumar Goel, HUF, upon the Respondent's assurance that seven categories of services,
namely, (i) Research on e-mail, (ii) Research on SMS, (iii) Call & Trade, (iv) Dedicated
Dealer, (v) Call with Expert, (vi) Portfolio Update, and (vii) Stock-specific Research, would
be made available to him during the subsistence of the plan.
3.2 On 11.11.2020, the said plan was renewed/extended for a further period, under Plan
Code "VSP-103" (recorded by the District Commission, on the material before it, as
"SVSP-32"), upon payment of a further sum of Rs. 12,980/- (Rupees Twelve Thousand
Nine Hundred Eighty only), the Respondent having represented telephonically that the
promised services would continue to be provided.
3.3 On the Respondent's own subscription-utilization records, annexed by it as Annexure
Rj-1 and Annexure-5 to its Reply filed before the State Commission, only 2.23% of the sum
of Rs. 5,90,000/- and 5.98% of the sum of Rs. 12,980/- stood utilized as on 05.07.2021,
leaving Rs. 5,76,430/- and Rs. 12,204/- respectively -- aggregating to Rs. 5,88,634/- --
unconsumed and lying with the Respondent.
3.4 By letter/notice dated 07.12.2021, the Appellant called upon the Respondent for refund
of the unutilized amount, together with compensation, alleging that the promised services
had not been provided. It is the Appellant's case that the said letter/notice was never
replied to or denied by the Respondent.
3.5 On 14.01.2022, the Appellant instituted Complaint Case No. 10 of 2022 before the
District Commission, praying, inter alia, for (i) refund of the unutilized subscription of Rs.
6,02,980/-, (ii) compensation of Rs. 6,10,000/-, (iii) interest @ 24% p.a., (iv) litigation costs
of Rs. 1,00,000/-, (v) return of an earlier subscription of Rs. 1,33,045/-, (vi) costs of Rs.
10,000/- for delaying proceedings, and (vii) a direction restraining the Respondent from
charging brokerage on delivery trades.
3.6 Notice of the Complaint was duly served upon the Respondent; the Respondent,
however, did not file a written reply before the District Commission and was accordingly
proceeded against ex-parte vide Order dated 06.07.2022.
3.7 By Order dated 31.03.2023, the District Commission dismissed the Complaint in its
entirety, holding that the Appellant had failed to discharge the onus of proving deficiency in
service, relying upon the ratio of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in
SGS India Ltd. v. Dolphin
International Ltd.
, AIR 2021 SC 4849.
3.8 Aggrieved, the Appellant preferred a Review Application dated 26.04.2023 before the
District Commission, which came to be dismissed vide Order dated 23.05.2023, the District
Commission holding that no error apparent on the face of the record had been made out.
 3.9 The Appellant thereafter preferred First Appeal No. A/292/2023 before the State
Commission. The Respondent, for the first time, entered appearance through counsel and
filed a detailed Reply resisting the Appeal. Both parties filed written submissions; the
Respondent additionally relied upon
B.F. Pushpaleela Devi v. State of A.P.
, 2002 (3) CTC
513 [reported as (
2002) 5 ALT 103] and SGS India Ltd. v. Dolphin International Ltd.
, 2021
SCC OnLine SC 879. By the impugned Order dated 20.08.2025, the State Commission
dismissed the First Appeal and upheld the Orders of the District Commission dated
31.03.2023 and 23.05.2023.
3.10 Aggrieved by the concurrent dismissal of his Complaint, Review Application and First
Appeal, the Appellant has preferred the present Second Appeal before this Hon'ble
Commission.
4. The operative and reasoning portion of the Order dated 31.03.2023 passed by the
District Commission in Complaint Case No. 10 of 2022 reads as under:
"8. This Commission has gone through the material
 available on record and it is seen that the complainant
 has availed of the services of the OP for the first time
 on 08.11.2019 for a period of one year, thereafter the
 same was renewed on 11.11.2020 for a period of three
 years. Though the complainant has stated in the
 complaint that he is an old man, it is evident from the
 material that the complainant is a well-informed, well-
 read person who has availed of some other agencies
 also other than the OP for trading in shares.
9. It is also seen from the record that the both the plans
 availed of by the complainant were different in their
 services. Apart from one, the complainant has not
 placed on record any document on record to show that
 he had written to the OP complaining of the services of
 the OP and it is also not clear as to why the
 complainant would avail the services of the OP in
 subsequent year after being dissatisfied with their
 services in the earlier year.
10. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in the matter of
SGS
 India Limited vs Dolphin International
AIR 2021 SC
 4849 has held the following: 'The onus of proof that
 there was deficiency in service is on the complainant. If
 the complainant is able to discharge its initial onus, the
 burden would then shift to the Respondent in the
 complaint.'
11. It is therefore, upon the complainant to initially
 discharge its onus to prove that there was deficiency in
 service on the part of OP. This Commission has gone
 through the pleadings and documents filed by the
 complainant and find that complainant has not been
 able to discharge this onus. Therefore, the present
 complaint is dismissed being devoid of any merits."
5. The Review Application dated 26.04.2023 preferred by the Appellant against the Order
dated 31.03.2023 was dismissed by the District Commission vide Order dated 23.05.2023.
The said Review Order, as reproduced in the impugned Order of the State Commission,
reads as under:
"A review application dated 26.04.2023 has been filed
 by the complainant seeking review of order dated
 31.03.2023. The complainant has filed the review...
Section 40
of the consumer protection act is
 reproduced below: -
'40. Review by District Commission in certain cases:-
 The District Commission shall have the power to review
 any of the order passed by it if there is an error
 apparent on the face of the record, either of its own
 motion or on an application made by any of the parties
 within thirty days of such order.'
 A Review application can only be entertained if there is
 an error on the face of the record. The complainant has
 filed the present review in disguise of an appeal and
 has stated that deficiency on the part of the OP stands
 proved and that the complainant had written to the OP
 regarding the deficiency vide letter dated 07.12.2021
 which the Commission has not considered.
 It is seen from the order passed dated 31.03.2023 that
 the order categorically states 'apart from one, the
 complainant has not placed on record any document to
 show that he had written to the OP complaining of the
 services of the OP....' This Commission had
 considered all the documents which were placed by
 complainant on record which is reflected in the order
 'apart from one'. In this case there seems no error
 which is apparent on the face of record and therefore
 review is dismissed."
6. The State Commission, after reproducing the Orders of the District Commission and the
Review Order in extenso, recorded its own reasoning and operative conclusions as under:
"9. We have perused the material available on record
 and heard the counsel appearing on behalf of the
 parties.
10. The main question that falls for our consideration is
 whether the District Commission erred in dismissing the
 Complaint case as well as Review Application of the
 Appellant.
11. On perusal of record, we find that the Appellant has
 subscribed to plan Code 'V-13' for trading in shares by
 paying Rs. 5,90,000/- to the Respondent for the said
 subscription. Further, we find that the Appellant has
 alleged before the District Commission as well as
 before this Commission that the said subscription was
 taken by the Appellant on the pretext that it would be
 valid for 10 years, however, the said subscription was
 valid only for one year and the Appellant further got the
 subscription renewed for three years on 11.11.2020
 with the plan code namely 'VSP 103' instead of 'V 13'.
12. Furthermore, we find that the Appellant has failed to
 show any document or any evidence in order to show
 that initial plan code 'V 13' was valid for 10 years,
 therefore, no presumption can be raised in this regard
 and the District Commission has rightly observed the
 same in the impugned order dated 31.03.2023.
 13-14. ... The Appellant herein submitted that these
 services were not provided by the Respondent and also
 wrote a letter dated 07.12.2021 to the Respondent
 regarding the said complaint. However, on perusal of
 the record, we find that...
15. ...the Respondent vide its reply has submitted that
 all the promised services has been provided to the
 Appellant and the record of the same has been
 annexed as Annexure - 3 of the reply to the present
 Appeal. Furthermore, we find that the Respondent has
 stated that the Appellant has continued to trade through
 the Platform of the Respondent and the last trading
 were done by the Appellant on 09.08.2024. Therefore,
 from the above, we find that the Appellant has failed to
 carve any deficiency of service on the part of the
 Respondent before the District Commission as well as
 before this Commission.
16. In view of the above, we are in agreement with the
 reasons given by the District Commission and fail to
 find any cause or reasons to reverse the findings of the
 District Commission. Therefore, we uphold the order
 dated 31.03.2023 and 23.05.2023 passed by the
 District Commission Disputes Redressal Commission-
 II...
17. Resultantly, the present Appeal stands dismissed
 with no order as to costs.
18. Application(s) pending, if any, stand disposed of in
 terms of the aforesaid judgment."
7. In the present Second Appeal, the Appellant has prayed as under:
"6. PRAYER
 It is humbly prayed that this Hon'ble Commission may
 be pleased to -
(i) Quash the Orders Dated 20.08.2025, 31.03.2023
 and 23.05.2023 and allow this Appeal.
(ii) Direct the Respondent to Refund the unutilized
 Advance Brokerage [Subscription] of Rs. 5,76,430/-
 (97.77%) out of Rs. 5,90,000/-.
(iii) Direct the Respondent to Refund unutilized
 Advance Brokerage Rs. 12,204/- (94.02%) out of Rs.
 12,980/-.
(iv) Direct the Respondent to pay Compensation of Rs.
 7,00,000/- to Appellant.
(v) Direct the Respondent to pay interest @ 24% p.a. till
 the Refund and Compensation is paid.
(vi) Direct the Respondent to pay Cost of Rs. 2,00,000/-
 to Appellant for forcing this Litigation.
(vii) Direct the Respondent to return earlier Subscription
 of Rs. 1,33,045/-.
(viii) Direct the Respondent not to charge for any Sale
 or Purchase of Shares from Appellant [Delivery
 Brokerage].
(ix) Pass such other order as deemed fit and proper in
 the interest of justice."
8.1 SUBMISSIONS ON BEHALF OF THE APPELLANT

8.1.1 The Appellant, appearing in person, at the outset submitted that the impugned Order
of the State Commission, insofar as it proceeds upon the two judgments cited by the
Respondent, namely,
B.F. Pushpaleela Devi v. State of A.P.
and
SGS India Ltd. v. Dolphin
International Ltd.
, rests on an incorrect application of the said precedents to the facts of the
present case.
It was submitted that the decision in
B.F. Pushpaleela Devi v. State of
A.P.
, reported at (2002) 5 ALT 103, is a Full Bench decision of the High Court of Andhra
Pradesh rendered on the question whether an intra-court appeal lies, under Clause 15 of
the Letters Patent, against an order of a learned Single Judge declining to review his own
judgment. The concluding paragraph of
the said decision
, on which reliance was placed,
reads as under:
"54. By the impugned order, the learned single Judge
 found no error apparent on the face of the record or any
 clerical mistake warranting review of the order."
8.1.2 It was submitted that the aforesaid paragraph merely records a finding on the
maintainability of an appeal against a review-refusal order, and has no bearing on any
question of deficiency in service, refund of subscription, or unfair trade practice arising
under the
Consumer Protection Act, 2019
. According to the Appellant, the citation of this
decision by the Respondent, and its reproduction in the record of the proceedings before
the State Commission, was misconceived and irrelevant to the controversy at hand.
8.1.3 As regards the second decision, the Appellant submitted that
SGS India Ltd. v.
Dolphin International Ltd.
, 2021 SCC OnLine SC 879, turns on its own facts, namely, a
 disputed allegation of negligence in the certification of the quality of a consignment at the
time of loading. The paragraph specifically relied upon by the Appellant reads as under:
"25. In the absence of any proof of negligence on the
 part of the appellant at the time of loading of the
 consignment, the appellant cannot be held responsible
 if at the port of destination, the products specifications
 were not the same as certified by the appellant at the
 time of loading of consignment."
8.1.4 It was submitted that the ratio extracted above is confined to a case where the very
occurrence of negligence was in dispute and required affirmative proof; it does not,
according to the Appellant, apply to a case such as the present, where the extent of
utilization of the advance subscription is not a matter of dispute at all, but stands
established from the Respondent's own record, viz. Annexure Rj-1 and Annexure-5 to its
Reply. The Appellant submitted that treating the two claims -- one for a disputed act of
negligence, and the other for return of an admitted, unutilized balance -- as governed by
an identical evidentiary standard, was erroneous.
8.1.5 The Appellant next relied upon
Lucknow Development Authority v. M.K. Gupta
,
(1994) 1 SCC 243, for the proposition that the
Consumer Protection Act
is a social-welfare
legislation to be construed liberally and purposively in favour of the consumer. The
paragraphs relied upon read as under:
"Under our Constitution sovereignty vests in the people.
 Every limb of the constitutional machinery is obliged to
 be people oriented. No functionary in exercise of
 statutory power can claim immunity, except to the
 extent protected by the statute itself. Public authorities
 acting in violation of constitutional or statutory
 provisions oppressively are accountable for their
 behaviour before authorities created under the statute
 like the commission or the courts entrusted with
 responsibility of maintaining the rule of law."
"The provisions of the Act thus have to be construed in
 favour of the consumer to achieve the purpose of
 enactment as it is a social benefit oriented legislation.
 The primary duty of the court while construing the
 provisions of such an Act is to adopt a constructive
 approach subject to that it should not do violence to the
 language of the provisions and is not contrary to the
 attempted objective of the enactment."
8.1.6 Reliance was also placed upon
Baldev Raj Chadha v. Union of India
, (1980) 4
SCC 321 : AIR 1981 SC 70, for the proposition that arbitrary exercise of power, including
by a quasi-judicial authority, cannot be sustained. The paragraph relied upon reads as
under:
"...The right to retire is not absolute, though so worded.
 Absolute power is anathema under our constitutional
 order. 'Absolute' merely means wide, not more. Naked
 and arbitrary exercise of power is bad in law. These
 essentials once grasped, the appellant's submissions
 become self-evident."
8.1.7 The Appellant further relied upon the decision of this Hon'ble Commission in
Subhash Chander Mahajan & Anr. v. Parsvnath Developers Ltd., CC No.
144 of 2011,
decided on 05.05.2014 (reported at 2014 SCC OnLine NCDRC 11), for the proposition
that refund together with compensation, interest and litigation costs has been granted by
this Commission where an opposite party failed to honour the conditions on which monies
were collected from a consumer.
The subsequent decision of this Commission in
Puneet
Malhotra v. Parsvnath Developers Ltd., Consumer Complaint No.
232 of 2014, decided on
29.01.2015, records the effect of
the said decision
thus:
"...in another case,
CC/144/2011, Subhash Chander
 Mahajan Vs. Parsvnath Developers Ltd., another
Bench of
 this Commission directed the opposite party to pay interest
 @ 18% per annum, besides compensation amounting to Rs.
 7.00 lacs and cost of litigation amounting to Rs. 2.00 lacs, in
 a case where refund was sought..."
8.1.8 Lastly, the Appellant relied upon the decision of the Rajasthan State Consumer
Disputes Redressal Commission in Sarvajeet Singh v. Batra Hotel, Rawatsar, decided
on 22.01.2004, for the proposition that a trader who levies an unjustified cost upon a
consumer, or retains an amount without corresponding justification, is guilty of unjust
enrichment and unfair trade practice. The paragraph relied upon reads as under:
"Adoption of such practice which leads to levy of
 unjustified cost on the goods sold to the customer with
 a view to get oneself unjustly enriched amounts to
 'unfair trade practice' besides being restrictive trade
 practice."
8.1.9 On the strength of the above decisions, the Appellant submitted that Condition No. 8
appended to the subscription plan, permitting the Respondent to discontinue the plan "for
any reason without giving prior intimation to clients," is a one-sided and restrictive
condition, that the retention of the unutilized balance of the advance subscription by the
Respondent amounts to unjust enrichment, and that the impugned Orders of the fora
below, having failed to appreciate the above, are liable to be set aside and the reliefs
prayed for granted in full.
8.2 SUBMISSIONS ON BEHALF OF THE RESPONDENT

8.2.1 Learned Counsel for the Respondent, adopting the Reply filed to the Second Appeal,
submitted that the grounds raised by the Appellant are baseless and that the District
Commission and the State Commission have concurrently and correctly found that the
onus of proving deficiency of service lay upon the Appellant and was not discharged by
him. It was submitted that the Appellant had continued to trade on the Respondent's
platform as late as 09.08.2024 without demur, that the renewal of the plan and the PAN-
based telephonic confirmation constituted valid and informed consent, and that the claim
for refund, raised after having availed of and enjoyed the services over an extended
period, was an afterthought unsupported by any contemporaneous complaint save the
solitary letter dated 07.12.2021.
8.2.2 In support of its case, the Respondent relied upon the very same two decisions
noticed above, namely,
B.F. Pushpaleela Devi v. State of A.P.
and
SGS India Ltd. v.
Dolphin International Ltd.
, as recorded in Para 8 of the impugned Order of the State
Commission. As regards the first decision, the Respondent relied upon the same
concluding paragraph extracted above, for the limited proposition that a review can only be
entertained where there is an error apparent on the face of the record:
"54. By the impugned order, the learned single Judge
 found no error apparent on the face of the record or any
 clerical mistake warranting review of the order."
8.2.3 As regards the second decision, the Respondent placed principal reliance upon the
following paragraphs of
SGS India Ltd. v. Dolphin International Ltd.
, 2021 SCC OnLine
 SC 879, for the proposition that the onus of proving deficiency in service lies squarely upon
the complainant, and that in the absence of discharge of such onus, the opposite party
cannot be held liable:
"19. The onus of proof of deficiency in service is on the
 complainant in the complaints under the
Consumer
 Protection Act, 1986
. It is the complainant who had
 approached the Commission, therefore, without any
 proof of deficiency, the opposite party cannot be held
 responsible for deficiency in service."
"22. ...The onus of proof that there was deficiency in
 service is on the complainant. If the complainant is able
 to discharge its initial onus, the burden would then shift
 to the Respondent in the complaint. The rule of
 evidence before the civil proceedings is that the onus
 would lie on the person who would fail if no evidence is
 led by the other side."
8.2.4 On the strength of the above, the Respondent submitted that the concurrent findings
of the District Commission and the State Commission, both of which applied the ratio in
SGS India Ltd.
(supra) to hold that the Appellant had failed to discharge the initial onus of
proving deficiency in service, warranted no interference, and that the Second Appeal,
being devoid of merit, was liable to be dismissed.
ISSUES ARISING FOR CONSIDERATION
9. On a conspectus of the pleadings, the impugned Orders and the submissions advanced,
the following issues arise for the consideration of this Commission:
(i) Whether the impugned Order dated 20.08.2025 of the State Commission suffers from
any error warranting interference in the exercise of this Commission's jurisdiction under
Section 51(2)
of the Act?
(ii) Whether the two judgments relied upon before the State Commission, viz.
B.F.
Pushpaleela Devi v. State of A.P.
and
SGS India Ltd. v. Dolphin International Ltd.
, were
correctly applied so as to defeat the entirety of the Appellant's claim?
(iii) Whether the District Commission and the State Commission erred in treating the
Appellant's claim for refund of the unutilized/unconsumed balance of the advance
subscription as indistinguishable from, and as governed by the same onus-of-proof
 standard applicable to, a claim of qualitative "deficiency in service"?
(iv) Whether, on the admitted documentary record -- including Annexure Rj-1 and
Annexure-5 to the Respondent's own Reply -- the Appellant is entitled to refund of the
unutilized balance of the advance brokerage/subscription paid by him, irrespective of the
fate of his other claims?
ANALYSIS

10.1 We have heard the Appellant in person and Learned Counsel for the Respondent,
and have perused the record, including the impugned Orders, the pleadings and the
documents relied upon by both sides.
10.2 We may first deal with the two decisions relied upon before the State Commission.
The decision in
B.F. Pushpaleela Devi v. State of A.P.
, reported at (2002) 5 ALT 103, is a
Full Bench decision of the High Court of Andhra Pradesh, rendered on the question
whether an intra-court appeal under Clause 15 of the Letters Patent lies against an order
of a learned Single Judge declining to review his own judgment. The ratio of that decision
turns entirely upon the appeal ability of an order refusing review under the Letters Patent,
and has no bearing upon any question of deficiency of service, refund of subscription, or
unfair trade practice arising under consumer law. We find force in the Appellant's
submission that reliance on this decision, being unconnected with the subject matter of the
lis, does not advance the case of the Respondent, and, with respect, ought not to have
found mention as a precedent bearing upon the merits of a consumer dispute of this
nature.
10.3 The second decision,
SGS India Ltd. v. Dolphin International Ltd.
, 2021 SCC
OnLine SC 879 (Civil Appeal No. 5759 of 2009, decided on 06.10.2021), lays down the
well-settled position, reiterating the earlier decision in
Ravneet Singh Bagga v. KLM
Royal Dutch Airlines & Anr.
, (2000) 1 SCC 66, that:
"19. The onus of proof of deficiency in service is on the
 complainant in the complaints under the
Consumer
 Protection Act, 1986
. It is the complainant who had
 approached the Commission, therefore, without any
 proof of deficiency, the opposite party cannot be held
 responsible for deficiency in service."
"22. ...The onus of proof that there was deficiency in
 service is on the complainant. If the complainant is able
 to discharge its initial onus, the burden would then shift
 to the Respondent in the complaint. The rule of
 evidence before the civil proceedings is that the onus
 would lie on the person who would fail if no evidence is
 led by the other side."
10.4 The correctness of the above proposition is not in doubt, and it binds this
Commission. What has, however, escaped the attention of the fora below is that the ratio
in
SGS India Ltd.
(supra) was rendered in the context of a claim of negligence in the
performance of a specific, disputed act -- namely, whether the inspection agency had
been negligent in certifying the quality of a consignment of groundnuts at the time of
loading, a matter on which the evidence was squarely at issue between the parties and
which the complainant therein was unable to substantiate. The present case, in the limited
respect with which we are concerned, stands on a different footing. The claim for refund of
the unutilized balance of the advance subscription is not founded upon a disputed
allegation of negligence in the performance of a specific act; it is founded upon an
arithmetical and documentary fact -- the extent of utilization of the subscription -- which is
not disputed by the Respondent and which stands established from the Respondent's own
record, viz. Annexure Rj-1 and Annexure-5 to its Reply, a record which the District
Commission itself noticed while recording the facts of the case (Order dated 31.03.2023,
Para-5). Where a fact stands established from the opposite party's own record, the
question of onus becomes academic; the initial onus, even if it lay upon the Appellant,
stood discharged the moment the Respondent's own annexures corroborated the extent of
utilization of the subscription.
10.5 It bears emphasis that a claim for refund of an unutilized advance is, in substance,
distinguishable from a claim of qualitative "deficiency in service." A subscriber who pays an
advance sum for services to be rendered over a defined period, and who is subsequently
found, on the service-provider's own record, to have utilized only a marginal fraction of that
advance, has an independent and freestanding entitlement to the return of the
unconsumed balance, irrespective of whether a separate case of qualitative deficiency in
the services actually rendered is made out. To hold otherwise would permit a service-
provider to retain monies for which no corresponding service has been, or realistically can
be, rendered -- a result productive of unjust enrichment of the service-provider at the
expense of the consumer, which the beneficial and welfare character of the Act was never
intended to countenance.
10.6 In this connection, it is apposite to recall the observations of the Hon'ble Supreme
Court in
Lucknow Development Authority v. M.K. Gupta
, (1994) 1 SCC 243, wherein it
was authoritatively held as under:
"The provisions of the Act thus have to be construed in
 favour of the consumer to achieve the purpose of
 enactment as it is a social benefit oriented legislation.
 The primary duty of the court while construing the
 provisions of such an Act is to adopt a constructive
 approach subject to that it should not do violence to the
 language of the provisions and is not contrary to the
 attempted objective of the enactment."
10.7 Adopting the above constructive and purposive approach, we are of the considered
view that the fora below fell into error in treating the entirety of the Appellant's claim --
including the discrete claim for refund of the unutilised balance -- as governed by, and
defeated under, the onus-of-proof standard properly applicable to disputed allegations of
negligent or qualitatively deficient performance. The unutilised balance, amounting to Rs.
5,76,430/- (out of Rs. 5,90,000/- paid on 11.11.2019) and Rs. 12,204/- (out of Rs. 12,980/-
paid on 11.11.2020), aggregating to Rs. 5,88,634/-, stands substantiated by the
Respondent's own record and remains, on the material placed before us, unrebutted by
any evidence to the contrary.
10.8 We may also note, without returning any final finding thereon since it is not essential
to the disposal of this Appeal, that Condition No. 8 appended to the subscription plan,
which purports to permit the Respondent to discontinue the plan "for any reason without
giving prior intimation to clients," is a term of a kind that has attracted judicial disapproval
where included in a standard-form contract offered to a consumer with no meaningful
power to negotiate its terms. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in
Central Inland Water
Transport Corporation Ltd. v. Brojo Nath Ganguly
, AIR 1986 SC 1571 : (1986) 3 SCC
156, held as under:
"...the courts will not enforce and will, when called upon to
 do so, strike down an unfair and unreasonable contract, or
 an unfair and unreasonable clause in a contract, entered
 into between parties who are not equal in bargaining
 power... It will also apply where a man has no choice, or
 rather no meaningful choice, but to give his assent to a
 contract or to sign on the dotted line in a prescribed or
 standard form..., however unfair, unreasonable and
 unconscionable a clause in that contract or form or rules
 may be."
We leave the question of the validity of Condition No. 8 open for examination in an
appropriate proceeding, as the limited relief we propose to grant does not require its
adjudication.
10.9 We may further note that the retention of monies received for a purpose that has
substantially failed, without corresponding consideration having passed, offends a basic
principle of restitution recognised in Indian law even outside the specific framework of
consumer legislation -- that a person who has received money without corresponding
consideration cannot, in equity and good conscience, be permitted to retain it. This
principle finds recognition in the interpretation placed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court on
Section 72
of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, in
Sales Tax Officer, Banaras v. Kanhaiya
Lal Mukundlal Saraf
, AIR 1959 SC 135, wherein it was observed as under:
"
Section 72
of the Indian Contract Act is in the following
 terms: 'A person to whom money has been paid, or anything
 delivered by mistake or under coercion, must repay or return
 it.' As will be observed the section in terms does not make
 any distinction between a mistake of law or a mistake of
 fact. The term 'mistake' has been used without any
 qualification or limitation whatever and comprises within its
 scope a mistake of law as well as a mistake of fact."
"Held, that the term 'mistake' in
Section 72
of the Indian
 Contract Act comprises within its scope a mistake of law as
 well as a mistake of fact and that, under that section a party
 is entitled to recover money paid by mistake or under
 coercion, and if it is established that the payment...has been
 made by the party labouring under a mistake of law, the
 party receiving the money is bound to repay or return it
 though it might have been paid voluntarily, subject,
 however, to questions of estoppel, waiver, limitation or the
 like."
10.9.1 Though rendered in the context of recovery of tax paid under a mistake of law, the
decision illustrates the wider principle, applicable with equal force by analogy, that the law
does not permit one party to retain money received by it where the corresponding basis for
such retention -- whether described as consideration, contractual entitlement, or service
actually rendered -- does not, in fact or in law, subsist. This general principle reinforces,
 rather than displaces, the more specific and beneficial relief available to a consumer under
the Act.
10.10 We accordingly hold that the District Commission and the State Commission erred in
dismissing the Complaint and the First Appeal, respectively, in their entirety, without
independently examining and granting the Appellant's claim, at the very least, for return of
the unutilized/unconsumed balance of the advance subscription paid by him, which stands
established from the record and is not seriously in dispute. To this limited extent, the
impugned Orders cannot be sustained and are liable to be set aside. We, however, find no
material on the record before us to independently sustain the Appellant's further claims for
compensation, interest at the rate claimed and the other ancillary reliefs prayed for, which
were declined by the fora below for want of proof of deficiency in the qualitative sense, and
we decline to disturb the said findings on those limited aspects.
Order
11. In view of the foregoing discussion, the Second Appeal is allowed in part, in the
following terms:
(i) The Order dated 20.08.2025 passed by the State Commission in First Appeal No.
A/292/2023, and the Order dated 31.03.2023 and the Review Order dated 23.05.2023
passed by the District Commission in
Complaint
Case No. 10 of 2022, are set aside.
(ii) The Respondent is directed to refund to the Appellant the unutilized/unconsumed
balance of the advance brokerage/subscription paid by him, namely, Rs. 5,76,430/- (out of
Rs. 5,90,000/- paid on 11.11.2019) and Rs. 12,204/- (out of Rs. 12,980/- paid on
11.11.2020), aggregating to Rs. 5,88,634/- (Rupees Five Lakh Eighty-Eight Thousand Six
Hundred Thirty-Four only), within a period of eight weeks from the date of receipt of a copy
of this Judgment.
(iii) The Respondent will also pay Rs.25,000/- as litigation cost to the Appellant.
(iv) Pending application(s), if any, stand disposed of in terms of the aforesaid directions.
(v) A copy of this Judgment be uploaded on the website of this Commission and sent to
 the parties, and the file be consigned to the record room in accordance with the Rules.
